sentences.text: Banguela oberlii is the only known species of an extinct azhdarchoid pterosaur from the Early Cretaceous period found in modern-day Brazil. This creature had an estimated skull length of about 2 feet and a wingspan of over 12 feet.

The defining feature of this animal is the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — which consists of the symphysis, or fused front end, of the lower jaws. This preserved symphysis measures 273 mm in length and curves upwards with a short depression at the upper rear end. The front bottom edge of the symphysis is sharp but lacks a true crest, and the fossil fragment contains no teeth or tooth sockets.
The genus name Banguela comes from a Brazilian Portuguese word meaning "toothless one," often used affectionately for elderly women. The species name oberlii honors the collector Urs Oberli.
Banguela is unique among dsungaripteroid pterosaurs due to its total absence of teeth.

The holotype fossil was acquired by Swiss collector Urs Oberli from the Chapada do Araripe region. The holotype specimen NMSG SAO 251093 was found in the Romualdo Formation and dates to the Albian stage.

In 2005, André Jacques Veldmeijer and colleagues described the fossil as a species of Thalassodromeus. Jaime Headden and Hebert Bruno Nascimento Campos named and described Banguela as a separate genus in 2015.

Tooth loss likely evolved independently at least four times among pterosaurs, as seen in groups like pteranodontids, nyctosaurids, and azhdarchoids. If tooth loss occurred frequently, Banguela may indicate it developed via the growth of horned rhamphothecae and progressive tooth reduction until teeth became useless.
In 2015, Headden and Campos classified Banguela in the family Dsungaripteridae in a basal position.
Banguela lived during the Early Cretaceous period. Banguela lived between 119.57 and 113.2 million years ago.
The holotype dates from the Aptian to Albian stages.

Researchers disputed the classification of Banguela as a dsungaripterid because no unambiguous traits of that group were found in the type specimen. A 2018 study suggested Banguela was actually a species of Thalassodromeus and assigned it to the clade Thalassodromidae. In 2020, McPhee and colleagues argued that Banguela is a valid genus belonging to the Chaoyangopteridae.
